title: When the knots of the heart are cut
theme: When all the knots of the heart are cut here, then the mortal becomes immortal. This much is the teaching.

words.context: Śaṅkara: cognitions of ignorance, «अविद्याप्रत्यया इत्यर्थः»; Raṅgarāmānuja: attachment, aversion and the like, «रागद्वेषादयो»

sandhi.type: aḥ before a; aḥ before a voiced consonant; i before an unlike vowel; t before h
sandhi.rule: The visarga of -aḥ becomes u before a, giving o, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) with P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), and the following a is merged, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति); the avagraha marks it. -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च). i before an unlike vowel becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि). t before h becomes d, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते), and the h after it becomes dh, P. 8.4.62 (झयो होऽन्यतरस्याम्).

morphology.note: Passive present of pra + √bhid, ‘are split apart’: the knots are cut, the image being of a tight bond loosened.
etāvat, ‘this much, so much’, with the suffix -vat after the pronoun etad. Śaṅkara stresses ‘only this much’; Madhva’s text lacks hi (corrections.json).

translation.literal: When all the knots of the heart are cut here, then the mortal becomes immortal: this much indeed [is] the teaching.
translation.readable: When all the knots of the heart are cut here and now, then the mortal becomes immortal. That is the whole of the teaching.

syntax: A temporal clause yadā … prabhidyante with its subject granthayaḥ, answered by atha martyo ’mṛto bhavati as in 2.3.14; then a closing verbless clause, etāvad dhy anuśāsanam.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the cognitions of ignorance, tight as knots, such as ‘I am this body, this wealth is mine, I am happy or unhappy’, «अहमिदं शरीरं ममेदं धनं सुखी दुःखी चाहमित्येवमादिलक्षणाः». Raṅgarāmānuja: attachment, aversion and the like, hard to loosen as knots, «ग्रन्थिवत् दुर्मोचा: रागद्वेषादयो». Madhva, in a verse in his comment: the knots of false knowledge, «मिथ्याज्ञानग्रन्थिभिस्तु».

Śaṅkara: this much and no more is the instruction of all the Vedāntas; one should not suspect anything further. Raṅgarāmānuja: this much is the seeker’s own task; what the next verse describes, the going out by the crown channel and the path of light, is not the seeker’s doing but the Lord’s, «न साधकस्य कृत्यम्, किन्तु उपासनप्रीतभगवत्कृत्यम्».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: Regular: 16 and 16 syllables. Madhva’s text, without hi, would have fifteen in the second line.

beginner: This verse repeats the promise of the last one with a new image: knots in the heart. When all of them are cut, here in this life, the mortal becomes immortal, and that, it says, is the whole teaching. Śaṅkara says the knots are the mistaken thoughts that tie us, such as ‘I am this body, this money is mine, I am happy, I am miserable’. When one knows oneself as Brahman, these knots are cut and the desires that grew from them die at the root. He takes ‘this much is the teaching’ as the summary of all the Upaniṣads. Raṅgarāmānuja says the knots are attachment and aversion, and that ‘this much’ is all the seeker has to do: what comes after, the journey at death described in the next verse, is the Lord’s work, not ours. A Muṇḍaka verse uses the same image.
analogy: A parcel tied with many knots cannot be opened by pulling harder; it opens when each knot is undone.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: When all the knots of the heart are cut here, the mortal becomes immortal; this much is the teaching.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The verse tells when desires are destroyed at the root: when the knots of the heart, that is the intellect, are split, here while one lives, «हृदयस्य बुद्धेरिह जीवत एव ग्रन्थयो». The knots are the cognitions of ignorance, «अविद्याप्रत्यया इत्यर्थः», such as ‘I am this body’; when the knowledge ‘I am Brahman’ arises they perish, and the desires born of them perish at the root. ‘This much’ means this much and no more, the teaching of all the Vedāntas, «अनुशासनम् अनुशिष्टः उपदेशः सर्ववेदान्तानामिति वाक्यशेषः».

commentary.q: Raṅgarāmānuja: the seeker’s part and the Lord’s
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Repeating the point for emphasis, the verse concludes: the knots are attachment, aversion and the like, «ग्रन्थिवत् दुर्मोचा: रागद्वेषादयो». This much is what the seeker is to be taught to do; the going out by the crown channel and the path of light described next are not the seeker’s act but the Lord’s, pleased by meditation, «वक्ष्यमाणमूर्धन्यनाडीनिष्क्रमणार्चिरादिगमनादिकं न साधकस्य कृत्यम्, किन्तु उपासनप्रीतभगवत्कृत्यम्».

commentary.q: Madhva: the knots of false knowledge
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: In a verse in his comment: when one is wholly freed from the knots of false knowledge, one reaches immortality, and the teaching is for that, «मिथ्याज्ञानग्रन्थिभिस्तु नितरां मुच्यते यदा । तदाऽमृतत्वमेवैति तदर्थं चानुशासनम्».

commentary.q: The Muṇḍaka’s knot of the heart
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: The Muṇḍaka has the same image: «भिद्यते हृदयग्रन्थिश्छिद्यन्ते सर्वसंशयाः».

advaita.text: The knots are cognitions of ignorance, «अविद्याप्रत्यया इत्यर्थः»; when they are cut, desire perishes at the root, and this is the whole teaching of the Vedānta.

visistadvaita.text: Cutting the knots of attachment and aversion is the seeker’s part; the journey that follows is the Lord’s doing, «उपासनप्रीतभगवत्कृत्यम्».

dvaita.text: The knots are those of false knowledge, «मिथ्याज्ञानग्रन्थिभिस्तु नितरां मुच्यते यदा».

schools.disagreement: The knots are cognitions of ignorance (Śaṅkara), attachment and aversion (Raṅgarāmānuja), or false knowledge (Madhva). ‘This much is the teaching’ is for Śaṅkara the sum of the Vedānta; for Raṅgarāmānuja the limit of the seeker’s own task.

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka’s knot of the heart, split when the highest is seen.
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s twin of the preceding verse, whose second line this one repeats up to bhavati.

contemporary.text: Śaṅkara’s examples of the knots are plain: ‘I am this body, this is mine, I am happy, I am miserable’. Much ordinary distress is tied to such knots. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What thought about yourself feels most like a knot?
reflect.deeper: Are the knots mistaken beliefs, or attachments? Does cutting one cut the other?
reflect.practice: When you next say ‘I am …’ or ‘this is mine’, notice what it ties you to.

flags.note: Madhva’s text lacks hi in etāvad dhy anuśāsanam (corrections.json).
The knots as cognitions of ignorance (Śaṅkara), attachment and aversion (Raṅgarāmānuja) or false knowledge (Madhva); ‘this much’ as the whole teaching or as the seeker’s part.
